title: Limits of Resolution: The Rayleigh Criterion
lead: Diffraction spreads the light from every point source into a fuzzy spot surrounded by rings, so the images of two sources that are close together overlap and blur into one. By the Rayleigh criterion, two images are just resolvable when an angle of 1.22 λ/D separates them. The criterion gives the finest detail a telescope, an eye or a microscope can show, and how far a beam of finite diameter spreads.
summary_html:
• Diffraction limits resolution.
  • For a circular aperture, lens, or mirror, the Rayleigh criterion states that two images are just resolvable when the center of the diffraction pattern of one is directly over the first minimum of the diffraction pattern of the other.
  • This occurs for two point objects separated by the angle $\theta = 1.22\frac{\klam}{\kDap}$, where $\klam$ is the wavelength of light (or other electromagnetic radiation) and $\kDap$ is the diameter of the aperture, lens, mirror, etc. This equation also gives the angular spreading of a source of light having a diameter $\kDap$.

exercises.prompt: What is the relationship between the width (W) of the central diffraction maximum formed through a circular aperture and the size (S) of the aperture?

options: W can increase or decrease as S decreases.
W can neither increase nor decrease as S decreases.
answer.hint: The first minimum lies at $\theta = 1.22\klam/\kDap$, so ask what happens to that angle as the aperture grows.

exercises.prompt: Light from two sources passes through a circular aperture to form images on a screen. State the Rayleigh criterion for the images to be just resolvable and draw a figure to visually explain it.

answer.solution: The Rayleigh criterion states that two images are just resolvable when the center of the diffraction pattern of one is directly over the first minimum of the diffraction pattern of the other. For a circular aperture of diameter $\kDap$ this happens when the sources are separated by the angle $\theta = 1.22\klam/\kDap$. A good drawing shows the two sources, the rays from each crossing at the aperture, and on the screen two intensity curves, each with a broad central maximum and small side maxima, placed so that the peak of one sits exactly on the first zero of the other. The sum of the two curves then shows a slight dip between two peaks, which is just enough to tell that there are two sources.

exercises.prompt: A beam of light always spreads out. Why can a beam not be created with parallel rays to prevent spreading? Why can lenses, mirrors, or apertures not be used to correct the spreading?

answer.solution: Every beam has a finite diameter $\kDap$, and light of wavelength $\klam$ confined to that width diffracts, spreading at an angle of about $\theta = 1.22\klam/\kDap$. The spreading comes from the wave nature of light and the limited width of the beam, not from any imperfection in the rays, so no arrangement of rays can remove it. A lens, mirror or aperture also has a finite diameter, so the light leaving it diffracts in the same way; the best any of them can do is make the beam wider, which makes the spreading angle smaller but never zero.

exercises.prompt: The 300-m-diameter Arecibo radio telescope pictured in Figure 27.28 detects radio waves with a 4.00 cm average wavelength. (a) What is the angle between two just-resolvable point sources for this telescope? (b) How close together could these point sources be at the 2 million light year distance of the Andromeda galaxy?

parts.hint: Use $\theta = 1.22\klam/\kDap$ with both lengths in meters.
Multiply the angle by the distance, $\ks = r\theta$.

exercises.prompt: Diffraction spreading for a flashlight is insignificant compared with other limitations in its optics, such as spherical aberrations in its mirror. To show this, calculate the minimum angular spreading of a flashlight beam that is originally 5.00 cm in diameter with an average wavelength of 600 nm.

answer.hint: A beam of diameter $\kDap$ spreads at $\theta = 1.22\klam/\kDap$.

exercises.prompt: A telescope can be used to enlarge the diameter of a laser beam and limit diffraction spreading. The laser beam is sent through the telescope in opposite the normal direction and can then be projected onto a satellite or the Moon. (a) If this is done with the Mount Wilson telescope, producing a 2.54-m-diameter beam of 633-nm light, what is the minimum angular spread of the beam (the angle between the beam's maximum and its first zero)? (b) Neglecting atmospheric effects, what is the size of the spot this beam would make on the Moon, assuming a lunar distance of $3.84\times 10^{8}\;\text{m}$?

parts.part: (b) the diameter of the spot on the Moon
parts.hint: The beam spreads by $r\theta$ on each side of its axis, so the spot is about twice that across.

exercises.prompt: What is the minimum diameter mirror on a telescope that would allow you to see details as small as 5.00 km on the Moon some 384,000 km away? Assume an average wavelength of 550 nm for the light received.

answer.hint: Find the angle from $\ks = r\theta$, then solve $\theta = 1.22\klam/\kDap$ for $\kDap$.

exercises.prompt: (a) The planet Pluto and its Moon Charon are separated by 19,600 km. Neglecting atmospheric effects, should the 5.08-m-diameter Mount Palomar telescope be able to resolve these bodies when they are $4.50\times 10^{9}\;\text{km}$ from Earth? Assume an average wavelength of 550 nm. (b) In actuality, it is just barely possible to discern that Pluto and Charon are separate bodies using an Earth-based telescope. What are the reasons for this?

answer.solution:
(a) Yes. Should easily be able to discern.

(b) The fact that it is just barely possible to discern that these are separate bodies indicates the severity of atmospheric aberrations.
